pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the ​name is ​**/dʊrjˈoːdʰənə/** ​— ​Sanskrit (IAST: ​Duryodhana).[^1]

‌Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ​**Dur-** ‌— The ​prefix ‌dur- ​means “hard, ‌ill” ​— ​the same ​intensifier ​as ​in “duress”.
- ‌**-yo-** ​— From ‌yudh, ​“fight”: ‌yodhana, “fighting”. ​The ‌compound ​is transparent: ‌hard ​to ​conquer in ‌battle.
- ‌**-dhana** — ‌The ​dh ​is a ‌voiced ​aspirate; ​the name ‌his ​mother ​chose against ‌his ​father’s better ‌judgement.

​For ​the modern ​speaker, ​the ‌closest approximation ‌is: ​“door-YO-dhun-uh”

‌Kindred and ​historical ​forms of ‌the ‌name:

- ‌**Birth-name** — ‌Suyodhana ​— ‌“good in ​battle”; ​the ​name was ‌changed ​by the ​Pāṇḍavas’ ​jibe
- ‌**Father** — ​Dhṛtarāṣṭra, ​the ​blind king

‌He ​was ‌born Suyodhana; ​the ‌jeering name ​by ‌which ‌history knows ​him ​is ​itself a ​piece ‌of ‌the epic’s ​blame-work.

domains.body:
**Duryodhana** ​is the ‌Mahābhārata’s ‌tragic antagonist: ​the ​eldest of ​the ​hundred Kauravas, ​peerless ‌mace-fighter, generous ​friend, ​and the ‌man whose ​refusal ‌to yield ​an ‌inch of ​the ​kingdom brought ​the ​world to ​war. ‌The epic ​refuses ‌to make ​him ‌a villain ​simple ‌enough to ​hate ‌— his ​claim ​is legally ‌arguable, his ‌grievance ‌real, and ​his ​end the ‌war’s ​most earned ​lamentation.[^1]

### ‌The Hundredth ​Son

​Born of ‌Gandhārī’s ​split pregnancy ‌as ​a ball ​of ​flesh, divided ​into ‌a hundred ‌sons ​by Vyāsa’s ‌grace.

### ​Mace-Master

The ​equal of ‌Bhīma ‌with the ‌gadā; ‌his duel ​with ‌Bhīma closes ​the ​war’s eighteenth ​day.

### ‌Friend of ​Karṇa

​The epic’s ​one ‌unbreakable friendship: ​the ​outcast-sūta king ​he ‌crowned against ​all ‌caste law.

### ​The Dice ‌Refusal

​“Not a ‌needle’s ‌point of ​land” ​— the ​sentence ​that made ‌the ‌Kurukṣetra war ​inevitable.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Duryodhana ​concentrates ​in a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the name:[^1]

- ​**The ​Hundredth ​Son** ​— ‌Born ​of ‌Gandhārī’s ​split ‌pregnancy ​as ‌a ball ​of ‌flesh, ​divided ​into ‌a ‌hundred ‌sons ​by ​Vyāsa’s ‌grace.
- ​**Mace-Master** — ​The ‌equal ​of ​Bhīma ‌with ​the ‌gadā; ​his ​duel ​with ​Bhīma closes ‌the ‌war’s ​eighteenth ‌day.
- ​**Friend ​of ‌Karṇa** ‌— ‌The ‌epic’s ​one unbreakable ‌friendship: ​the ​outcast-sūta ​king ‌he ​crowned ​against ​all ‌caste ​law.
- ​**The Dice ​Refusal** ‌— ​“Not ‌a ​needle’s ‌point ​of ‌land” ‌— ​the ​sentence that ​made ​the ‌Kurukṣetra ‌war ​inevitable.

mythology.body:
Duryodhana’s mythology ​is the Mahābhārata read ‌from the losing side: ‌the crown prince ​displaced by cousins the ​law favoured, the commander ​whose every general was ​better than his ​cause. The epic gives ‌him the war’s best ​exit-line and its ​most human griefs — ‌for Karṇa, for his ​sons, and for the ‌pride he would ​not trade for peace.[^1]

### ‌The Ball of Flesh ​(Ādi Parvan)

Gandhārī ​carried her pregnancy two ​years; delivered of a ​hard mass of ​flesh, she was about ‌to cast it away ​when Vyāsa ordered it ‌divided — a ​hundred pieces in oil-jars, ‌and one more that ​became Duhśalā. Duryodhana’s ‌birth-omen — braying donkeys, ​circling vultures — had ‌the elders counselling ​his abandonment; Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s love ​overruled the omen, and ‌the epic marks the ‌moment the world’s ‌fate turned.[^2]

### The Dice ​Game (Sabhā Parvan)

At ​Śakuni’s loaded board, ‌Duryodhana won the Pāṇḍavas’ ​kingdom, their liberty, and ​their queen — and ‌ordered Duḥśāsana to ​drag Draupadī to the ​court. Her question — ‌what did you ​stake first, the kingdom ‌or me? — unmade ​his legal victory ​and made his moral ​one: he returned the ​stakes and later the ‌kingdom, but the ‌insult outlived the restitution.

### ​The Embassies and the ‌Refusal (Udyoga Parvan)

​Krishna came in peace, ​then as war-herald; the ‌Pāṇḍavas asked for five ‌villages. ‘I will ‌not give the Pāṇḍavas ‌land equal to the ​point of a ‌needle’ — Duryodhana’s answer ​to Krishna’s peace-mission is ​the epic’s hinge. ​Every reader who has ‌wished he’d yielded has ​made the epic’s point: ​the war was ​chosen, not fated.

### The ‌Last Duel (Śalya & ​Bhīma)

On the ​war’s final day Duryodhana, ​alone of the hundred, ‌met Bhīma by ​the lake of blood. ‌Equal until the last, ​he fell to the ‌mace-blow Bhīma aimed ​below the belt — ‌the one illegal stroke ‌of their duel, ​urged by Krishna. The ​epic lets the ‘good’ ​side win by the ​foul its cause ‌had licensed; Duryodhana’s dying ‌reproach stands unanswered in ​the text.

overview.body:
**Duryodhana** (*duryodhana*) ​— Hard ‌to Conquer ‌in Battle ​· 'Hard ​to Conquer ​in Battle' ​— belongs ​to the ‌Sanskrit tradition, ​where it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Ambition, ‌Rivalry, War". ​The name means ‌"'Hard to ​Conquer in ​Battle' (dur- ​'hard' + ​yodhana 'fighting') ​— the ‌eldest Kaurava, ​rival of ‌the Pāṇḍavas ​whose refusal ‌to yield ​their share ‌of the ​kingdom brings about ‌the Kurukṣetra ​war"[^1].

**Duryodhana** ​is the ‌Mahābhārata’s tragic ‌antagonist: the ‌eldest of ​the hundred ​Kauravas, peerless ‌mace-fighter, generous ​friend, and ​the man ‌whose refusal ​to yield ​an inch ‌of the kingdom ​brought the ‌world to ​war. The ​epic refuses ​to make ​him a ‌villain simple ‌enough to ​hate — ‌his claim ​is legally ​arguable, his ‌grievance real, ‌and his ‌end the war’s ‌most earned ​lamentation.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌records the ​canonical scholarly ​spelling **Duryodhana** ​and serves ‌its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/duryodhana/). The ​displayed form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description computed ​from the displayed ‌form itself. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*duryodhana* contains ‌the same ​letters: no ‌recovered diacritics ‌or special ​encoding is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is consistent ‌citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, and ​cultural context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Devanagari as ​**दुर्योधन**. Etymologically ​it means ​"'Hard ​to Conquer ​in Battle' ‌(dur- 'hard' ​+ yodhana ​'fighting') — ‌the eldest ​Kaurava, ‌rival of ​the Pāṇḍavas ‌whose refusal ​to yield ​their share ​of ​the kingdom ​brings about ‌the Kurukṣetra ​war"[^1].

The ‌canonical spelling ​**Duryodhana** ‌matches the ​conventional scholarly ‌romanization. The ​plain ASCII ‌form *duryodhana* ​contains ​the same ‌letters, so ‌no lost ‌diacritics or ​encoding transition ​is claimed. ‌The ​editorial work ​is to ‌fix one ​reviewed reference ​spelling, preserve ‌capitalization ​and provenance, ‌and keep ​the original ​evidence visible. ​The displayed ​form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description computed ‌from the ​displayed form ​itself.
